# Mine

Mine is a set of PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) to digitalize ones personal or professional life.
The key idea is to save everything in a repo as markdown files. This can be calendar entries,
diaries, markdowns extracted from voice recordings / pdfs / .. These .md files can easily be
ported to new apps without a vendor lock-in and are processed via an (AI) assistant to help you
plan your day, keep track of tasks, remind you of memories a.k.a. a second brain.

To keep complexity to a minimum each use-case lives in a separate folder. e.g. the calendar PWA
lives completely in a 'calendar' folder as does the zettelkasten and all the other apps. Each
folder contains a 'sample' folder with samples how the markdowns shall look, a REQUIREMENTS.md
describing how the PWA works and a TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md describing how it is built.

See [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) for how this is built, and
[TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md) for how it is checked.

## One app, one setup

Mine installs as **one** app on the phone, with one icon. The apps in the subfolders are pages
inside it, not separate installs.

This is what makes the central requirement work: **the GitHub repo and token are entered once,
in the main app, and every app in a subfolder uses them.** Verified on iPhone and Android.

## Main app

A tile per app: its `icon.svg` above its folder name.

Above the tiles, apps may contribute a summary. The calendar's shows today's entries and the
next one — which matters, because opening the app is the only reminder that works (see below).

## First run

1. Open the app URL and add it to the home screen (iOS: Share → Add to Home Screen;
   Android: menu → Install).
2. The setup screen asks for GitHub owner, data repo, branch, and a personal access token.
3. The app tests the connection and reports clearly if it fails.

Settings are stored on the device only. The token is never displayed again after entry, and the
app warns 14 days before it expires.

Two settings belong to Mine rather than to any one app, and the same two rows appear in the main
settings and in each app's: **theme** (system, light or dark) and **date format** (auto, which
follows the device's locale, or `dd.mm.yyyy`, or `mm/dd/yy`). Both default to following the
device, so Mine looks like the rest of the phone until you say otherwise.

One convention is the same in every app: **a save icon is green and a trashcan is red**, wherever
either appears — a trashcan is red even where it only clears one field of a form that has not
been saved, because the rule is the icon, not the consequence. A save keeps the weight of a
primary action and is a filled green button; a trashcan is a red glyph on no background. The `x`
that closes or abandons something is neither, and stays plain.

## Using it

- Changes appear instantly and are queued for GitHub in the background.
- A sync indicator shows: in sync / pending / error.
- Offline, the queue is kept and sent when you are back online or reopen the app.
- Editing the same entry on two devices never loses either version: the other device's version
  keeps the file, yours is kept beside it and flagged, and the sync indicator tells you there is
  something to review. Nothing is discarded and nothing is silently overwritten — but the app
  does not interrupt you to ask which to keep, because by then you are somewhere else.
- Everything works offline, including dates and search, because the app keeps a full local copy.

## Reminders

**Mine cannot notify you while it is closed.** No browser can schedule a notification for later;
this is a platform limitation, not a missing feature. Alerts are stored with each entry and
exported, and they fire while the app is open. The summary on the tile screen is the reminder.

## Updates

When a new version is deployed the app shows "Update ready — reload". It never updates while you
are in the middle of editing.

The banner appears only when the version waiting to take over genuinely differs from the one
running. A new worker can sit waiting while being identical to the active one, so "a worker is
waiting" is not the test — if it were, the banner would appear on an app with no update at all
and never go away. Reloading twice with no deploy in between must leave no banner.

## Privacy

Your data lives in a **private** repo. The app itself is public, but it contains no data, and the
token is scoped so that it can only touch the data repo.

content.content:
# Calendar

Calendar is an app of [Mine](../REQUIREMENTS.md) to manage your calendar. Every entry is one
markdown file in the data repo, so your calendar stays readable and portable without this app.

See [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) for the file format.

## What an entry holds

A title, a type — **event** or **task** — a start and end, a group, a location, participants,
alerts, and a free markdown body for the agenda, checklist or notes.

A task also carries a **stage** — `todo`, `doing` or `done` — and, optionally, a priority (1, 2
or 3) and an estimate in days. An event has none of the three. Stage is the only record of a
task's progress; there is no separate done flag.

A new task starts at `todo` with an estimate of **1 day**. Both are only defaults: either can be
changed before saving, and the estimate can be cleared away again, so `estimate` stays a key an
entry may simply not have — nothing writes one into a task that never carried one.

Entries can repeat, and a repeating entry can have single occurrences skipped, moved, retitled
or moved to another stage without affecting the rest.

## Layout

A navigation pane at the top and a big calendar window below it.

In the top pane, from left to right:

- Left/right buttons to move to the previous/next day, week, month, year or sprint, depending on
  the current view.
- The current day/week/month/year, with a small downward arrow for a dropdown date picker. The
  dropdown shows a month at a time, with its name top left and left/right arrows top right.
  Clicking the month name switches to a year grid of 9 years ending with the current one, whose
  arrows page by 9 years. In the kanban view the label reads `Sprint 7 · 19 Jan – 1 Feb` and the
  dropdown picks a sprint.
- A button to jump to today.
- A dropdown to filter by group. Each group shows its colour. This is a view filter and is
  remembered per device; groups are *named and coloured* in settings, not here.
- `D` `W` `M` `Y` `K` to choose the view: day, week, month, year, kanban.
- A return arrow back to the Mine tile screen.
- A gear button that opens settings.

All views show **seven columns beginning with the configured first day of the week**, with
Saturday and Sunday tinted wherever they land. A Saturday task has to be visible.

When *show calendar weeks* is on, each week row carries its ISO 8601 week number in a left
gutter, separated from the days by a thin vertical rule. The number is always ISO, whichever
day the week is set to start on. ISO weeks run Monday to Sunday, so a row beginning on Sunday
holds one day of one ISO week and six of the next; the number shown is the one the rest of the
row is in.

A `+` button adds an entry. It defaults to today when today is in view, and otherwise to the
first day on screen — in the kanban, to the first day of the selected sprint, in its todo
column.

## Views

- **Year** — every month, each with a weekday header row and one row per week. The current day
  is highlighted. A day with entries takes the background colour of its group, split between
  colours if there are several — a year grid has no room for anything else. Clicking a day shows
  that day's entries.
- **Month** — one row per week. Entries appear inside each day cell as small lines carrying the
  title on the group's background colour, sorted by time, all-day items first. On desktop a timed
  entry's line is prefixed with its time; on a phone it is the title alone, because seven columns
  across a phone have no room for both and the title is the part worth reading — the time is one
  tap away in the day preview. A cell shows at most four on desktop and two on a phone, then
  `+N`. Tasks have a rectangular icon on the right to move them straight to done. Clicking empty
  space in a cell creates an entry; clicking an entry opens it.
- **Week** — columns are the days, rows are the 24 hours.
- **Day** — the week view for a single day, with more detail per entry.
- **Kanban** — below.

Groups switched off in the filter are not shown in any view.

### The day preview

Clicking a day opens that day's entries as a list, each one tappable. Its top right carries a
small `+` to add an entry on that day and a small `x` to close it — not full-width buttons.

## Entry popup

A row of icon buttons at the top, from left to right:

- `T` for task, a calendar page for event. Choosing one deselects the other; the default is
  event.
- On a task only: `S` for **stage**, `P` for **priority**, `E` for **estimate**. On an event the
  three are not there at all, because an event has none of them.
- A circular-arrows button for **repetition**.
- A ball for **category**.
- A pin for **location**.
- A bell for **alerts**.
- A person for **participants**.
- `D` for **details** — the markdown body.
- Then, right-aligned: an `x` to close and discard, a trashcan to delete the entry, and a disk
  to save it.

An icon whose field is set is shown enabled: a brighter background in dark mode, a darker one in
light mode. So the row doubles as a summary of what the entry carries.

**Stage, priority and estimate are not like the others.** They are three small values rather than
fields with a form each, so they are edited in the row itself and they show their value rather
than merely whether they have one:

- `S` cycles `todo` → `doing` → `done` on each tap, tinted with that stage's kanban colour —
  red, yellow, green. There is no stage popup.
- `P` cycles none → 1 → 2 → 3 → none, showing the digit on that priority's chip colour.
- `E` is the one that opens a popup, because a number has to be typed. It shows the day count as
  `2d`, exactly as a kanban card does — which is also what keeps it apart from the priority
  digit beside it.

So the enabled rule above is about the six field icons; these three are always legible instead.
They sit in the row so that a task that is not on a board still carries the two fields a kanban
card edits.

Each of the six field buttons opens its own popup, and every popup has the same three buttons:
a trashcan that clears that one field, an `x` that abandons the sub-edit, and a disk that commits
the value into the entry form and lights the icon. **A sub-popup never writes to the repo**,
with the single exception noted under Category.
Nothing is written until the entry popup's own disk, so one entry edit is one commit, and the
entry popup's `x` discards the staged fields along with everything else. This is also what makes
a brand-new entry work, since it has no file for a sub-popup to write to.

Below the icon row:

- the title field;
- the start and end fields;
- then one row per field that is set, in the order of the icons above — so a location that has
  been given appears at the bottom. Each row has a pen to reopen its popup and a trashcan to
  clear it.

Saving **closes the popup and returns to the calendar immediately**; the push to GitHub runs in
the background and is reported in the sync line, not in the popup.

### Repetition

A dropdown, not an RRULE field:

```
does not repeat · daily · weekly · every 2 weeks ·
monthly on the x-th · monthly on the x-th weekday · yearly
```

below it an **ends** control: never, on a date, or after a number of occurrences.

Files may be hand-written or imported, so a rule the dropdown cannot express — `the last Friday
of the month`, `Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays` — is shown as a non-selectable **custom** state
displaying the rule as text, with a note that choosing an option will replace it. Saving the
entry without touching the dropdown leaves the rule untouched. No hand-written rule is ever
silently rewritten.

### Category

The groups, each with its colour, and a `+ add` button. Adding a group asks for a label and a
colour; its stored name is derived from the label and never shown, which is why relabelling or
recolouring later touches no entry. Adding one writes `groups.md` immediately rather than staging
it: that is a different file from the entry, and a category must not disappear because the entry
it was created for was discarded. A pen edits a group, a trashcan deletes it — and entries
still naming a deleted group render grey.

## Kanban

Three columns — **todo** (red), **doing** (yellow), **done** (green) — holding one sprint's
tasks. Every task is a card and every card is a task; events never appear.

A sprint is a date range, not a stored field: sprint 1 starts on the *kanban first week start
date* and each one runs for the *kanban interval*. A task's sprint is whichever range its start
falls in, so the number can never disagree with the date, and moving a card to another sprint
is exactly a change of its start and end. Both settings therefore live in the data repo, not on
the device — if they differed between two devices the same card would be in different sprints.

A repeating task contributes one card per occurrence inside the sprint. Moving one records an
override for that occurrence alone; the rule itself is never rewritten.

Each column header shows its state, its colour and a card count. The sprint selector and a
filter icon (category, assignee, priority) sit in the top pane, because one board shows one
sprint.

A card shows:

- a top row with a trashcan to delete, a pen to edit, the title, and `<` `>` to move it to the
  previous or next stage — `<` disabled in todo, `>` disabled in done;
- below it two lines of the markdown body;
- on the right a priority chip (1 red, 2 orange, 3 yellow), the estimate in days, and the sprint
  number. Clicking any of the three changes it: the priority chip cycles 1 → 2 → 3, and the
  estimate and the sprint ask for a number. Changing the sprint moves the task's start and end
  into that sprint's range, keeping its offset within the sprint and its time of day.

On desktop all three columns are shown and a card can be dragged between them. On a phone one

# Mine — test requirements

What has to be checked before a change ships, and how. [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md) says
what the apps do; this says how we find out whether they still do it.

There is no CI and no test framework. `test/run.sh` drives a real browser against the real app
and prints one line per check, so running it is the whole of it:

```
test/run.sh                 the checks
test/run.sh --shot DIR      the checks, and a screenshot of each view into DIR
```

It needs `chromium` and node 20 or newer on the PATH, installs nothing, and writes nothing into
the repo. A failing check prints what it got and what it wanted, and the script exits non-zero.

## Why a browser and not unit tests

Almost everything that has actually broken here is a layout or a wiring fault — a grid track
that will not shrink, a button that stops being wired when its markup moves, a key written into
the frontmatter that should have been left out. None of those show up in a function test. The
model arithmetic that *is* worth testing in isolation (dates, sprints, recurrence expansion) is
pure and lives in `calendar/data.js`, whose `buildModel` takes files rather than reading them,
so it can be exercised from node against the same markdown the browser mirrors.

## How the harness works

`test/serve.py` serves the working tree, plus one synthetic route, `/__fixture.json`: a month of
entries generated for *the month the checks run in*. A fixture pinned to a fixed date would
leave the month view empty and every check green. It holds what has historically broken things —
long titles, timed entries, a day with more entries than a phone cell shows, all-day items, a
Saturday task.

`test/check.mjs` connects to Chromium over the DevTools protocol, seeds that fixture into
IndexedDB with a throwaway config, and drives the app by clicking the real buttons.

Two things about it are deliberate and easy to get wrong:

- **The viewport comes from `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride`, never from `--window-size`.**
  Chromium's headless mode lays the page out at a fixed 500 px and then *scales the capture* to
  the window size, so a 320 px screenshot taken with `--window-size` is a picture of a 500 px
  layout. It passes a fit check that a real phone fails. This cost an afternoon once.
- **The config holds a fake token.** The mirror is local, so every view renders from it; the
  push fails and writes a line into the sync indicator, which is correct and is not a failure.
  Nothing in the checks talks to GitHub, and no real token ever goes near a browser profile.

## What is checked

**Every view fits a phone.** Day, week, month, year and kanban, at 320 and 360 CSS px, in light
and dark. The test is `scrollWidth === clientWidth`: nothing may extend past the screen, in any
view, at any width. 320 px is the floor because it is the narrowest phone still in use and it
leaves room for Android's display-zoom setting, which makes a wider screen behave like a
narrower one.

This is the check that earns its keep. The month grid once ran 1239 px wide at a 360 px
viewport, and it looked perfect on a desktop the whole time: a `1fr` track is
`minmax(auto, 1fr)`, and a cell holding a `white-space: nowrap` title has that whole title as
its minimum width, so seven cells grew to fit their text rather than sharing the screen. A grid
cell that holds text needs `min-width: 0` or it does not shrink. The other offender was the
period label in the top pane, which is long enough in the week and sprint views to overflow a
narrow phone on its own.

**The entry popup's icon row.** That a new entry is an event and carries no stage, priority or
estimate; that choosing a task brings `S`, `P` and `E`; that `S` cycles through three stages in
three colours and back, that `P` cycles 1, 2, 3, none, each in its own colour, and that `E`
opens a popup prefilled with one day, shows `3d` once set and its letter once cleared; and that
switching back to an event takes all three away again.

**A save is green and a trashcan is red**, in the entry popup, its detail rows, a field
sub-popup, a kanban card and the settings panel. The check resolves `--good` and `--bad` from
the page rather than naming colours, so retheming does not break it.

**What a saved task writes.** A new task saved with nothing but a title must land as
`stage: todo` with `estimate: 1`, and a task whose estimate was cleared must have no `estimate`
key at all — not an empty one, and never `None`. This is the check that holds the file format
to [calendar/TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](calendar/TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md), and it reads the
file back out of the local mirror rather than trusting the form.

## A check must be able to fail

Before trusting a new check, break the thing it covers and watch it go red. A fit check written
against `--window-size` passes on a broken layout; a colour check that names `#0a7b3e` instead
of resolving `--good` passes when the token changes underneath it. Removing `min-width: 0` from
`.day` must turn the month fit checks red, and putting it back must turn them green.

## What the harness cannot tell you

Headless Chromium on a desktop is not a phone. It does not cover:

- **the real device** — a system font scale, a notch, a software keyboard, Safari's and
  Chrome's own quirks. Serve the tree with `python3 -m http.server` and open it from the phone
  on the same network, or push and open the live URL.
- **installing to the home screen, the service worker and the update banner** — these need an
  installed app over HTTPS. `spike/` covers the platform questions and needs no token.
- **GitHub sync**: pulling, the one-commit drain, conflict files, an expiring token. Only a real
  token against the real data repo exercises those, and that is done by hand.

A change to any of those three is checked on a device before it ships, and
[TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) records what was found and when.
